South Asia Snapshot - October 5, 2026

South Asia Navigates a Fragmenting World

Asia Society

Dear Readers,We mark two years of the South Asia Snapshot with this issue. While the world may not look entirely different from when we began, the region certainly has given us plenty to keep up with. Speaking of keeping up: we have just wrapped up a whirlwind month here in New York, where UNGA once again kept both Asia Society and the city’s traffic exceptionally busy. South Asian leaders descended on New York, bringing with them key priorities. So, let’s dive straight in.South Asia Comes to New YorkSouth Asian leaders arrived in New York in force, from Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah making his first official overseas trip, to Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman making his maiden visit to the United States as a premier.For Shah, the timing was particularly poignant. He arrived in New York just weeks after devastating floods hit Nepal. In his first address to the U.N. General Assembly, Shah called for climate justice and issued a broader warning about the consequences of climate change for the Himalayas. He asked whether the world had really heard the warning and called for a renewed commitment to “shared responsibility and solidarity.”Shah put forward a concrete regional proposal: a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India, and China, and focused on improving cross-border cooperation and disaster coordination. His view was that the Himalayas should become a laboratory for international cooperation.That is an important proposition for South Asia. Climate risks do not see borders, and neither do ecosystems that connect the region. Yet the institutions needed to manage these shared risks remain far less developed. As Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal also emphasized in his conversation with Asia Society Global President The Hon. Dr. Kevin Rudd AC, Nepal’s future cannot be charted in isolation, and the country stands ready to be a strategic bridge.Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman struck a similarly climate-focused note, calling for stronger global action at COP31. But his address also pointed to another emerging fault line: with artificial intelligence advancing rapidly, Rahman warned that today’s digital divide should not become tomorrow’s “artificial intelligence divide,” calling for technology transfer, skills development, and affordable access for developing countries.Sri Lanka’s Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath brought the conversation back to the Indian Ocean. He underscored that Sri Lanka’s prosperity is closely tied to the Indian Ocean and reiterated Colombo’s commitment to a peaceful order at sea.Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif highlighted Islamabad’s mediation efforts to facilitate dialogue between the United States and Iran. He also discussed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye, describing it as a collective commitment to defense, stability, and peace.Sharif once again thanked President Trump for what he described as his “resolute and visionary leadership” in relation to the India-Pakistan conflict last May. The remarks received attention in Washington, including from the White House Rapid Response X account.External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar placed India’s message within a broader critique of the pressures facing the Global South. He warned that “peace is not just the absence of war,” and argued that the developing world is confronting a “4F” crisis—food, fuel, fertilizer, and finance.Jaishankar also pointed to what he described as a growing “mindset of extreme competition,” arguing that finance, market access, supply chains, technology, resources, and connectivity are increasingly being used as instruments of geopolitical leverage. His prescription was greater diversification and de-risking, alongside reform of multilateral institutions.Why It Matters: There was a striking degree of convergence in the messages South Asian leaders brought to New York. They all made the case that South Asia is being asked to absorb the consequences of a climate crisis it contributed relatively little to creating. War is creating a similarly shared economic vulnerability. Conflicts beyond South Asia’s borders are increasingly transmitting directly into the region through energy prices, food and fertilizer supplies, shipping routes, and inflation. As Nepal’s Prime Minister Balen Shah aptly put it, “we have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food.”The sidelines of UNGA were perhaps even more revealing than the speeches themselves. India, consistent with its longstanding push for reform of the multilateral system, co-sponsored the launch of the Partners for Multilateralism (P4M) alongside Brazil, Canada, Kenya, Barbados, and the European Union. The grouping is an effort by a diverse set of middle powers to find common ground around strengthening a multilateral system under increasing global strain. Whether such initiatives can translate into meaningful institutional reform remains to be seen, but the search for new coalitions itself is telling.Following the signing of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA) by President Trump, Jaishankar met with Secretary of State Marco Rubio in New York to reiterate India’s concerns about the legislation. New Delhi has made clear that secondary sanctions and their effects on India would have consequences for the bilateral ties.Rubio is expected back in New Delhi later this month, while Prime Minister Modi is also expected to travel to the United States for the G20. Against that backdrop, Washington and New Delhi will have several opportunities to test whether recent tensions can be managed without derailing the broader relationship. Jaishankar was candid about the strains in his recent Asia Society conversation with Daniel Russel, noting that a trade agreement would help. In the meantime, Modi and Trump spoke by phone and agreed to take their “Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership” forward. The language remains warm, while the policy issues underneath are considerably more complicated. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer recently added that while constructive negotiations are ongoing, a U.S.-India trade deal is “not imminent.”Pakistan’s sidelines were also busy; Sharif met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in New York as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue to test Islamabad’s mediation efforts.At the same time, questions around the new Saudi-Pakistan-Türkiye security architecture are becoming harder to separate from the wider regional picture. Pakistan’s defense minister has indicated that Islamabad would support Saudi Arabia in the event of a conflict as tensions with the Houthis escalate.Dhaka and Islamabad have been steadily rebuilding relations after years of estrangement, while India-Bangladesh ties remain strained. That rapprochement was visible in New York, with Sharif and Rahman meeting and agreeing to advance bilateral ties.BRICS and India-China TiesBefore UNGA, BRICS leaders met in New Delhi, with Chinese President Xi Jinping making his first visit to India in seven years as the two sides cautiously work to stabilize ties.After BRICS foreign ministers failed to reach consensus in May, expectations for a joint declaration were low. Yet members ultimately agreed on one in a diplomatic win for host India. The language was carefully calibrated, calling for restraint in the Middle East and criticizing unilateral and secondary sanctions without naming specific countries.Why It Matters: BRICS’ ability to find common ground despite existing divergences is itself significant. The grouping is hardly unified on the Middle East, Ukraine, or the role of the West, but its members share concerns about an international order under strain. Modi, at the summit, called for the Global South to become “rule shapers” rather than “rule takers,” and unveiled a 10-point roadmap for global governance reform.The India-China engagement on the sidelines was consequential. Modi and Xi agreed to take a “strategic and long-term perspective” of the relationship and ensure that differences do not become disputes. At Asia Society, Jaishankar offered an assessment of the shift, noting that ties are considerably better than they were two years ago and arguing that a prolonged standoff benefits neither side because “third parties will take advantage.”Soon after BRICS came the closely watched Trump-Xi summit in Washington. For India, it will be important to see what the strategic stability between the United States and China means for its own leverage, especially as Washington’s economic pressures on New Delhi grow. The answer may be to preserve strategic flexibility and avoid being locked in either camp.Stay Tuned!Thank you for being on this journey with us for two years. So much more to come; keep reading and keep sharing.Warmly,Farwa Aamer
